Deposits of amyloid protein with apple-green birefringence on Congo red stain
Calcifications with a concentric, layered pattern
Aggregates of hemosiderin-laden macrophages
explanations: Incorrect - multinucleated giant cells surrounding necrotic debris describes granulomatous/caseous necrosis, not psammoma bodies.
Incorrect - apple-green birefringence on Congo red staining is characteristic of amyloid deposits, not psammoma bodies.

Correct - psammoma bodies are calcifications with a distinctive layered (concentric, laminated) pattern seen in certain neoplasms, such as thyroid cancer, and represent a form of dystrophic calcification.
Incorrect - hemosiderin-laden macrophages are a separate histologic finding unrelated to psammoma bodies.
questions.overview: Psammoma bodies are calcified structures with a characteristic concentric, layered appearance on microscopy, representing a form of dystrophic calcification. They are classically associated with certain neoplasms, including papillary thyroid carcinoma.

questions.stem: A patient with poor dietary intake and delayed wound healing is found to have vitamin C deficiency. Which of the following best explains the role of vitamin C in normal wound healing?
options: It is required as a cofactor for lysyl oxidase-mediated collagen cross-linking
It activates metalloproteinases to degrade type III collagen
It is necessary for collagen synthesis by fibroblasts
It stimulates VEGF-mediated angiogenesis at the wound site
explanations: Incorrect - collagen cross-linking is a copper-dependent (lysyl oxidase) process, not vitamin C-dependent, per the notes.
Incorrect - metalloproteinases are zinc-dependent enzymes; vitamin C's described role is in collagen synthesis, not activating collagen-degrading enzymes.
Correct - the notes state that vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is necessary for collagen synthesis, and its deficiency results in poor wound healing.
Incorrect - angiogenesis is primarily driven by VEGF and FGF, not vitamin C.
questions.overview: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is required for normal collagen synthesis by fibroblasts during wound healing. Deficiency impairs collagen production and results in poor wound healing, distinct from copper deficiency (impaired collagen cross-linking) and zinc deficiency (impaired collagen remodeling).

questions.stem: C-reactive protein is synthesized by the liver primarily in response to which cytokine, and performs which of the following functions?
options: IL-6; binds bacterial polysaccharides and activates complement
IL-1; inhibits iron transport via ferroportin
IFN-γ; activates macrophages to form giant cells
TNF-α; cross-links collagen fibers during wound remodeling
explanations: Correct - CRP is an acute phase reactant synthesized by the liver in response to IL-6 (produced by macrophages); it binds bacterial polysaccharides and activates the complement system.
Incorrect - inhibiting iron transport via ferroportin describes hepcidin, not CRP.
Incorrect - IFN-γ activates macrophages (M1), but this is not the CRP mechanism; giant cell formation is a granuloma feature, not a CRP function.
Incorrect - collagen cross-linking is performed by lysyl oxidase, unrelated to CRP or TNF-α.
questions.overview: C-reactive protein is an acute phase reactant produced by the liver in response to IL-6 released by macrophages during inflammation. It binds bacterial polysaccharides and activates complement, and chronically elevated levels are associated with coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man presents with tremor, dysarthria, and liver dysfunction. Slit-lamp exam reveals Kayser-Fleischer rings. Serum ceruloplasmin is low, and hepatic copper content is elevated. Which of the following best explains a mechanism by which excess free copper contributes to cellular injury in this disorder?
options: Free copper directly inhibits Na/K-ATPase, causing cellular swelling
Free copper activates caspases directly, triggering apoptosis
Free copper inhibits telomerase, accelerating cellular senescence
Free copper binds transferrin, preventing iron delivery to erythroid precursors
Free copper reacts with hydrogen peroxide via the Fenton reaction to generate hydroxyl radicals that damage lipids, proteins, and DNA
explanations: Incorrect - the notes describe copper toxicity via free radical (Fenton reaction) generation, not direct Na/K-ATPase inhibition.
Incorrect - copper's described mechanism of injury is free radical generation, not direct caspase activation.
Incorrect - telomerase inhibition is not a mechanism described for copper toxicity in the notes.
Incorrect - transferrin is an iron transport protein; copper is transported by ceruloplasmin, not transferrin.

Correct - excess free copper (normally bound by ceruloplasmin) participates in the Fenton reaction (H2O2 + Cu+ → Cu2+ + OH·), generating hydroxyl radicals that cause lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, and DNA damage, contributing to hepatocyte and neuronal injury in Wilson disease.
questions.overview: Wilson disease causes copper accumulation due to impaired biliary excretion, with low ceruloplasmin allowing free copper to accumulate in the liver, brain, and eyes (Kayser-Fleischer rings). Free copper, like free iron in hemochromatosis, drives the Fenton reaction, converting hydrogen peroxide into damaging hydroxyl radicals that injure cells via lipid peroxidation and macromolecule damage.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with painless, diffuse lymphadenopathy. Lymph node biopsy shows a nodular pattern of small, cleaved lymphocytes. Cytogenetic testing reveals a t(14;18) translocation resulting in overexpression of an anti-apoptotic protein located in the mitochondrial membrane. Which of the following mechanisms best explains how this overexpression contributes to malignancy?
options: The overexpressed protein prevents cytochrome c release from mitochondria, blocking caspase activation and allowing uncontrolled B-cell survival
The overexpressed protein binds Fas ligand, preventing death receptor signaling on the cell surface
The overexpressed protein inhibits NADPH oxidase, preventing reactive oxygen species generation
The overexpressed protein degrades p53, preventing cell cycle arrest
The overexpressed protein activates telomerase, allowing unlimited replication
explanations: Correct - follicular lymphoma is driven by BCL-2 overexpression, which keeps mitochondrial pores closed, prevents cytochrome c release, blocks caspase activation, and prevents apoptosis, leading to uncontrolled B-cell accumulation.
Incorrect - this describes the extrinsic Fas pathway, not the mitochondrial intrinsic pathway that BCL-2 regulates.
Incorrect - BCL-2 has no described role in inhibiting NADPH oxidase or respiratory burst.
Incorrect - BCL-2 does not act by degrading p53; it acts at the mitochondrial membrane.
Incorrect - telomerase activation is a separate hallmark of malignancy, not the mechanism of BCL-2 overexpression described in the notes.
questions.overview: Follicular lymphoma, a B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, is characterized by overexpression of BCL-2, an anti-apoptotic protein in the mitochondrial membrane. This prevents mitochondrial pore opening and cytochrome c release, blocking caspase activation and apoptosis, resulting in uncontrolled clonal B-cell growth.

questions.stem: Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) promotes wound healing and scar formation through which of the following combined effects?
options: Inhibits fibroblast migration to limit excessive scarring
Stimulates neutrophil chemotaxis and promotes fever via hypothalamic prostaglandins
Stimulates osteoclast-like transformation of vascular smooth muscle
Stimulates collagen production, inhibits collagen breakdown, and inhibits lymphocyte proliferation
explanations: Incorrect - TGF-β promotes, not inhibits, fibroblast activity and collagen production in wound healing.
Incorrect - neutrophil chemotaxis and fever are not the primary described functions of TGF-β in the notes.
Incorrect - osteogenic transformation of vascular smooth muscle is a feature of calciphylaxis, unrelated to TGF-β's wound healing role.

Correct - TGF-β, released by platelets, T cells, macrophages, and endothelial cells, stimulates collagen production, inhibits collagen breakdown, and is anti-inflammatory by inhibiting lymphocyte proliferation; TGF-β knockout mice show widespread inflammation.
questions.overview: TGF-β is released by platelets, T cells, macrophages, and endothelial cells during wound healing. It promotes scar formation by stimulating collagen synthesis and inhibiting its breakdown, while also acting as an anti-inflammatory signal that suppresses lymphocyte proliferation.

questions.stem: Bevacizumab is used in the treatment of certain cancers based on which of the following mechanisms of action?
options: Inhibition of cyclooxygenase, reducing prostaglandin-mediated pain
Inhibition of VEGF-A, reducing tumor angiogenesis
Inhibition of TNF-α, reducing granulomatous inflammation
Inhibition of BCL-2, promoting apoptosis of malignant cells
explanations: Incorrect - bevacizumab does not inhibit cyclooxygenase; that mechanism describes NSAIDs.
Correct - bevacizumab is a VEGF inhibitor used in cancer therapy that blocks VEGF-A-mediated angiogenesis, limiting the new blood vessel growth tumors need to grow.
Incorrect - anti-TNF drugs like infliximab and etanercept, not bevacizumab, are used for granulomatous/autoimmune inflammatory conditions.
Incorrect - bevacizumab targets VEGF, not BCL-2, which is a different therapeutic mechanism not described as bevacizumab's target in the notes.
questions.overview: VEGF-A is a key stimulator of angiogenesis, secreted by tumors to fuel their own vascular supply. Bevacizumab is a VEGF inhibitor used in cancer treatment to block this angiogenic signal, while ranibizumab, another VEGF inhibitor, is used in retinopathy.

questions.stem: Elevated hepcidin during chronic inflammation contributes to anemia of chronic disease through which of the following mechanisms?
options: Inhibiting erythropoietin receptor signaling in the bone marrow
Directly lysing red blood cells via complement activation
Binding ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages, trapping iron intracellularly as ferritin
Increasing transferrin synthesis to enhance iron delivery to erythroid precursors
explanations: Incorrect - the notes do not describe hepcidin acting on erythropoietin receptor signaling.
Incorrect - hepcidin's described mechanism is iron sequestration via ferroportin inhibition, not complement-mediated red cell lysis.

Correct - hepcidin, an acute phase reactant with antibacterial properties, binds ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages, trapping iron intracellularly as ferritin and limiting iron availability for erythropoiesis, contributing to anemia of chronic disease.
Incorrect - hepcidin limits iron availability; transferrin is a negative acute phase reactant whose levels fall, not rise, during inflammation.
questions.overview: Hepcidin is an acute phase reactant that has antibacterial properties by limiting iron availability to invading organisms. It binds ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages, trapping iron as intracellular ferritin, which contributes to the anemia of chronic disease seen with prolonged inflammatory states.

questions.stem: A patient with a bacterial infection has a complete blood count showing an increased proportion of immature band neutrophils along with increased total neutrophils. This finding is best described as which of the following?
options: Leukemoid reaction limited to lymphocytosis
Left shift, a normal bone marrow response to infection
Anaplasia of myeloid precursors
Karyorrhexis of circulating neutrophils
explanations: Incorrect - a leukemoid reaction can resemble leukemia due to marked leukocytosis but is not specifically defined as lymphocytosis; bacterial infections typically cause neutrophilia, not lymphocytosis.

Correct - a "left shift" describes an increase in immature neutrophil forms (bands) along with mature neutrophils in the blood, a normal response to infection driven by cytokines (TNF and IL-1) mobilizing cells from the bone marrow.
Incorrect - anaplasia refers to undifferentiated malignant cell growth, unrelated to a left shift.
Incorrect - karyorrhexis is a nuclear change seen in necrosis, not a description of circulating band neutrophils.
questions.overview: In response to infection, cytokines such as TNF and IL-1 stimulate the bone marrow to release neutrophils, including immature band forms, into circulation — a "left shift." This is a normal, expected response to bacterial infection and reflects increased granulopoietic demand.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with massive lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies show an increased number of double-negative T cells and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. Genetic testing identifies a mutation impairing a death-receptor pathway responsible for eliminating self-reactive lymphocytes. Which of the following best describes the expected downstream consequence of this mutation?
options: Defective p53 signaling prevents cell cycle arrest, resulting in unchecked epithelial proliferation
Defective NADPH oxidase impairs bacterial killing, leading to recurrent catalase-positive infections
Defective caspase-independent necrosis increases inflammatory cell death
Defective Fas-Fas ligand signaling impairs negative selection, resulting in excess lymphocyte survival and increased lymphoma risk
Defective BCL-2 downregulation increases mitochondrial apoptosis of thymocytes
explanations: Incorrect - ALPS is not described as a p53/cell cycle disorder; it is a death-receptor apoptosis defect.
Incorrect - this describes chronic granulomatous disease, a distinct entity from ALPS.
Incorrect - the notes describe ALPS as an apoptosis defect via Fas-FasL, not a necrosis-related process.

Correct - ALPS is caused by a defective Fas-Fas ligand extrinsic apoptosis pathway, impairing negative selection of self-reactive T cells in the thymic medulla, leading to lymphocyte overproduction, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and increased lymphoma risk.
Incorrect - ALPS involves decreased, not increased, apoptosis due to a defective extrinsic pathway, not altered mitochondrial signaling.
questions.overview: Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS) results from a defective Fas-Fas ligand pathway, which normally mediates negative selection of self-reactive T cells in the thymic medulla. Impaired apoptosis leads to lymphocyte accumulation, causing lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, autoimmune disease, and an increased risk of lymphoma.
